channel.title: Road Guide: Day 2 coast route
channel.description: Day 2 coast: Guerneville → Jenner → Bodega Bay → Tomales Bay → Point Reyes Station → Stinson Beach → Muir Woods → Golden Gate → SFO. Play episodes in order as you drive.
channel.itunes:author: Wine Country Road Guide

item.title: 01. Korbel: Bohemian brothers and California champagne
item.description:
Okay, wine lovers, up ahead is a winery that legally prints the word champagne on its labels, and France can't do anything about it.
It's Korbel, making sparkling wine here since 1882. It was started by Francis Korbel and his brothers, who came from Bohemia, and who also, randomly, started a satirical San Francisco magazine called The Wasp. They use the proper Champagne method, where the wine gets its second fermentation right in the bottle you buy.
So how do they get away with saying champagne? … Old American rules from the 1930s treat some place names as semi-generic, as long as the label

item.title: 02. Rio Nido: there is no Canyon Five
item.description:
Here's one of my favourite little places: Rio Nido, the river nest, a tiny resort village tucked into a redwood canyon. It was started in 1908 by a San Francisco lodge called the Eagles, so its first name was Eaglenest. In World War Two, its dance hall was packed with sailors on leave and big bands played there.
Okay, Julia, Adam, here's a weird one. The streets here are named Canyon One, Canyon Two, Canyon Three, Canyon Four, then Canyon Six and Canyon Seven. What's missing? … There's no Canyon Five! The story goes it's because of an accident on the road that became Canyon Six. Spooky.
And

item.title: 03. Guerneville: from Stumptown to resort town
item.description:
Ladies and gentlemen, Julia, Adam and our amazing driver: welcome to Guerneville! You made it! Woohoo!
Okay, pronunciation check. It's Gurn-vill. Locals even sell T-shirts that say Don't call it Guerneyville. So now you know.
Final quiz of the trip. The town's very first English name was a bit less pretty. Given that loggers cut down most of the giant redwoods here in the late 1800s, what do you think they called it? … Stumptown! And the parade every year is still called Stumptown Days. The redwoods grew so thick here that local legend says the valley had the densest amount of living stuff o

item.title: 04. Armstrong Redwoods: the trees the loggers missed
item.description:
If you've got an hour, go see the trees that the loggers missed: Armstrong Redwoods, just north of town. In the 1870s, Colonel James Armstrong saved the grove as a natural park. After he died, his daughter and another local family ran a whole campaign, with rallies and car caravans, to save this last bit of the old forest, and in 1917 the county bought it for 80,000 dollars.
Quiz: the tallest tree in there, the Parson Jones Tree, is a hundred yards from the entrance. How tall do you think it is? … More than 310 feet! That's taller than a thirty-storey building. And the oldest, the Colonel Arm

item.title: 05. The Pomo: the people of the Russian River
item.description:
This river is Pomo country. The Pomo lands once stretched from the Pacific coast all the way inland to Clear Lake. But here's the thing: the Pomo were never one single nation. They lived in small, independent bands linked by family, and they spoke seven related languages so different that speakers of one couldn't understand another.
Quiz: the name Pomo was originally the name of just one village. What do you think it meant? … Those who live at red earth hole! Probably after the red magnesite they mined to make beads, or the reddish soil. By 1877, English speakers were using it for everyone.

item.title: 06. Day two: river, ocean, redwoods, bridge
item.description:
Good morning, road-trippers! Day two. Mike's on driving duty, Adam and Julia are in charge of snacks, and I'm in charge of the chat.
Here's the plan. We follow the Russian River to the ocean, then drive down the wild Sonoma Coast to Bodega Bay, where Hitchcock made birds terrifying. Then either along Tomales Bay and Point Reyes, or inland through Petaluma, to the giant redwoods of Muir Woods. And finally over the Golden Gate Bridge, through San Francisco, to the airport.
Big trees first, if you've got an hour before you leave: Armstrong Redwoods is just north of Guerneville. The Parson Jones

item.title: 07. Bohemian Grove: the most exclusive campsite in America
item.description:
Okay, conspiracy fans, this one's for you. Just downstream at Monte Rio, hidden in the redwoods, is the Bohemian Grove: a 2,700-acre private campground owned by San Francisco's very exclusive Bohemian Club. Every July, powerful people from politics, business and the arts spend more than two weeks camping here.
It started innocently. In 1878, a bunch of journalists from the club had an overnight going-away party in the redwoods for an actor moving to New York. They had so much fun they did it again the next year, without him! Then the rich businessmen joined, and the money and the power follow

item.title: 08. The Russians in California
item.description:
We've met Russians again and again today: a river, a mountain, a farm near Graton. So here's the whole story.
Russian traders pushed east across Siberia and the North Pacific, and in 1799 they set up a colony in Alaska. Their business was fur, especially sea otters. From 1803, American ship captains took Alaska Native hunters down the California coast to hunt otters, and between 1805 and 1812 alone they gathered over 22,000 pelts.
In 1812 the Russians built their own base, Fort Ross, on the Sonoma coast, in the land of the Kashaya Pomo. It was super diverse: Native Californians, Native Alask

item.title: 09. Cannabis: California's other crop
item.description:
Wine isn't the only crop around here with a complicated legal history.
California has been at the front of cannabis politics for half a century. In 1972, it held the first ballot vote in the nation to legalise cannabis. Quiz: did it pass? … Nope! It failed. But in 1996, California became the first state to legalise medical cannabis, and in 2016, voters legalised recreational use, with 57 percent of the vote.
Legalisation turned out to be messy. Growers had to register and get permits, and more than half of the medical dispensaries closed. Legal businesses pay hefty taxes, while illegal growe

item.title: 10. Monte Rio and Duncans Mills: the railroad to the redwoods
item.description:
Picture this road with a little narrow-gauge train chugging along beside the river. From the 1870s, the North Pacific Coast Railroad ran from Cazadero, through Monte Rio and Duncans Mills, all the way down to the ferry at Sausalito. Remember that name, because the same railway also stopped at Valley Ford, Tomales, Marshall and Point Reyes Station. We're basically following its ghost all morning.
The business model changed twice. First, it hauled redwood lumber to build San Francisco: in 1877 Alexander Duncan set up a sawmill right here, and a town grew around it, with two hotels, a saloon, a

item.title: 11. Goat Rock: sea stacks, mammoths and the Goonies
item.description:
Movie quiz! Down on the right is Goat Rock Beach, with that huge flat-topped rock barely hanging on to the land. In 1985, a very famous adventure movie about a group of kids hunting for pirate treasure filmed its ending on this beach. Which one? … The Goonies! Goonies never say die.
Those rocks out in the sea are called sea stacks. For about 170 million years, an ocean plate was diving under North America, scraping off pillow lava, chert and sandstone and crushing it all into a jumble called mélange: hard blocks floating in softer, ground-up rock. The waves wash away the soft stuff and leave

item.title: 12. Jenner: the river meets the sea
item.description:
There it is! The Russian River meets the Pacific, right here at Jenner. Population: about a hundred and twenty.
The town is named after Dr. Elijah Jenner, a dentist and inventor from Vermont who came west for the Gold Rush in 1850. While mining, he designed a pump that could lift water a hundred feet. Quiz: when he applied for the patent, he sent in a model of the pump. What was so special about it? … It was made of pure gold! It's the only golden model the Patent Office has ever received. A proper Gold Rush flex.
Now watch the river mouth. In summer, the waves build a sandbar right across i

item.title: 13. The coast that is falling into the sea
item.description:
Quick-fire facts on the Sonoma Coast.
One: it's seventeen miles of state beaches from just north of Jenner down to Bodega Head.
Two: it's disappearing. Those soft bluffs lose one to three feet a year on average, more in a stormy winter.
Three: it's also rising. You're driving on a flat shelf above the beach called a marine terrace. It's old sea floor, lifted up over the ages. Some sea stacks are even stranded up on the terrace, away from the water, because they started life on the sea floor before it rose.
Four: people have lived here a very long time. Dozens of Coast Miwok and Pomo shell

item.title: 14. Why Highway 1 will never be a motorway
item.description:
Here's a bit of infrastructure politics, Mike, since you're the one stuck behind the camper vans. Ever wondered why Highway 1 is just one lane each way, even on busy summer weekends?
It's the law. The 1976 California Coastal Act specifically bans widening Highway 1 beyond one lane in each direction in the rural parts of the coastal zone. It's enforced by the California Coastal Commission, which has quasi-judicial control over development and public access along 1,100 miles of coastline. Its zone runs inland from about a thousand yards up to five miles. Inside it, almost anything, from a new h

item.title: 15. Lunch briefing: crab and oysters
item.description:
Lunch briefing, since I hear seafood is today's top priority.
Crab first. The working boats in Bodega Bay, coming up, go after Dungeness crab, one of the most important seafood catches on the whole West Coast, found from Alaska's Aleutian Islands down to near Santa Barbara. The fishery was started by San Francisco fishermen back in 1848, the year gold was found. By the early 1900s, rules said you could only keep hard-shelled male crabs at least six inches across, and those are still the rules today. Most are caught in baited wire pots on a buoy, and every pot must be tied on with a biodegrada

item.title: 16. Bodega Bay: Russians, Spaniards and a lot of movies
item.description:
Welcome to Bodega Bay! Fishing boats, salty air, and a harbor tucked behind that long headland.
It's named after Juan Francisco de la Bodega y Quadra, a Spanish naval officer who sailed in here in 1775. In 1793 the Spanish parked a little garrison here with four cannons, because they'd heard the English might turn up. They didn't, so the guns went home to Monterey. Then the Russians turned up instead! In 1809 they put up the first Russian buildings in California here, before building Fort Ross, and called the place Port Rumyantsev.
Hollywood loves it too: The Birds, The Fog, I Know What You

item.title: 17. The Birds: the true story behind the film
item.description:
Story time. In August 1961, the people of Capitola, a seaside town further down this coast, woke up to something out of a nightmare. Thousands of seabirds were dive-bombing their houses, crashing into cars and dropping half-eaten fish on people's lawns.
Alfred Hitchcock read about it. He was already working on a film based on a Daphne du Maurier story about birds attacking people, and he used the Capitola event as research. The result was The Birds, released in 1963 and set right here in Bodega Bay. Tippi Hedren, in her first film, drives up from San Francisco with a pair of lovebirds, and it

item.title: 18. The Hole in the Head: where the anti-nuclear movement was born
item.description:
Julia, this one's for you. Across the harbor is Bodega Head, and it has a hole in it, literally. It's where America's anti-nuclear movement is said to have been born.
In the late 1950s, the utility company PG&E planned to build a nuclear power plant on the headland, meant to be the first commercially viable one in the country. The fishermen worried about their livelihoods. A local landowner, Rose Gaffney, refused to sell, sued the company, and invited government officials to come and look at the fault lines on the site. In June 1963, protesters released 1,500 helium balloons, each carrying th

item.title: 19. From Bodega Head to Diablo Canyon and Livermore
item.description:
So where did California's nuclear story go next? Today it has exactly one working nuclear plant: Diablo Canyon, on the central coast, also run by PG&E. It makes about 8.6 percent of the state's electricity, and nearly a quarter of its carbon-free power. It was built less than a mile from a fault line nobody knew about at the time, and in 1981 nearly two thousand protesters were arrested there in just two weeks.
In 2016, PG&E said it would close it in 2024 and 2025, partly because California's rules give renewables priority. Then the grid operators warned of blackouts, 79 scientists wrote an o

item.title: 20. Bodega: rusty cannons and a famous schoolhouse
item.description:
This little village is Bodega, once called Bodega Corners, to tell it apart from the port down by the water. There were two Coast Miwok villages around here, and then in 1809 the Russians settled in the Salmon Creek valley.
When the Russians left, around 1843, John Sutter bought their land, including this area. The sale included some hunting rights, a small boat, several rusty cannons and some old muskets. Bargain. The same year, a Captain Stephen Smith built the first lumber mill on the West Coast near here. The town proper began in 1853 with a saloon, a blacksmith and a hotel, which is the

item.title: 21. Valley Ford and the Running Fence
item.description:
Tiny Valley Ford, population about a hundred and fifty, in rolling dairy country. The Coast Miwok had a village here called Ewapalt. There was a grain mill in the 1850s, and from 1876 the railway stopped here, so ranchers and fishers could ship their produce to San Francisco.
Quiz: in 1976, the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude built a giant artwork that passed right through Valley Ford, running from Cotati all the way to Bodega Bay. What was it? … A fence! Running Fence: a long white fabric fence over the hills and down into the ocean.
Two more. Guitarists, take note: Shubb, the company tha

item.title: 22. The Coast Miwok
item.description:
The land from the Golden Gate up to the Sonoma coast, and east to Sonoma Creek, was home to the Coast Miwok. That includes the hills around Sebastopol and Freestone and the lower Sonoma Valley.
They lived in small bands with no central government. In spring they headed to the coast for salmon, shellfish and seaweed. The rest of the year, acorns were the staple, plus deer and rabbit. Quiz: Coast Miwok hunters had a clever trick for sneaking up on deer. What do you think they did? … They rubbed themselves with a plant called Brewer's angelica to hide their scent! They also drank yerba buena tea

item.title: 23. Tomales: into Marin County
item.description:
Welcome to Marin County, and to Tomales, population just under two hundred.
The Coast Miwok had villages all around here, including one called Utumia, near the town. The post office opened in 1854, spelled Tomalles, with two L's, and later lost one. And the North Pacific Coast Railroad came through in the 1870s.
Tomales sits close to the San Andreas Fault, and you can still see the 1906 earthquake here, in the cemetery. One of the town's two cemeteries is older than the earthquake, and the damage to the old graves shows just how far the shaking reached.

item.title: 24. Tomales Bay: the fault you can sail on
item.description:
That long, skinny bay is Tomales Bay: fifteen miles long, about a mile wide, and only eighteen feet deep on average. In 1603, Spanish explorers from the Vizcaíno expedition saw it, assumed it was a river, and named it the Rio Grande de San Sebastián.
But it's not a river. It's a fault. Tomales Bay is a drowned stretch of the San Andreas Fault. Everything on the far side, the Point Reyes Peninsula, is on the Pacific Plate. You're on the North American Plate. The fault runs from here down the Olema Valley to Bolinas Lagoon, and this road follows it nearly the whole way.
The Coast Miwok had vil

item.title: 25. Marshall: oysters and a creamery
item.description:
This stretch of shore is Marshall, and if anyone's hungry: oysters.
The town is named after four Marshall brothers who started dairy farming here in the 1850s. There's still dairy, with the Straus Family Creamery based here, but the big business now is oysters and clams. The two biggest producers on Tomales Bay are Hog Island Oyster Company and Tomales Bay Oyster Company, and both sell straight to the public, with picnic tables right on this shore. If you stop, the local move is a bag of oysters at a table by the water.
Mike, a supply-chain footnote. Just across the peninsula, the Drakes Bay

item.title: 26. Why there are no wind turbines out there (yet)
item.description:
Adam, this one's yours. Out past Point Reyes is open Pacific, with some of the strongest offshore wind in the country. So where are all the turbines?
The problem is depth. The seabed off California drops away fast, so instead of fixed turbines on the seabed like in the North Sea, it needs floating ones. In 2021 the Biden administration approved large areas off the coast for floating wind farms, and in 2022 California set a target of 25 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2045. Then, this year, in 2026, the second Trump administration negotiated a series of deals that stopped three of the state's fi

item.title: 27. Francis Drake, New Albion and the porcelain clue
item.description:
Story time. On the 17th of June, 1579, the English captain Francis Drake sailed into a sheltered cove just over those hills. His ship, the Golden Hind, needed repairs after months of raiding Spanish towns and treasure ships up the Pacific coast, and he was about to sail home the long way, right round the world.
He stayed about five weeks, and got on well with the Coast Miwok who lived here. He named the land New Albion, partly because its white cliffs reminded him of England, and claimed it for Queen Elizabeth the First, nailing up a brass plate with a sixpence showing her face. On the 23rd o

item.title: 28. Point Reyes Station: the town that could not pick a name
item.description:
Welcome to Point Reyes Station, the little hub town for the Point Reyes peninsula.
It started as the end of the railway line. When the trains arrived in 1875, it was called Olema Station. Then, in 1891 alone, the name changed three times: first to Marin, then back to Point Reyes, then finally Point Reyes Station.
It used to be a real port on Tomales Bay, too. But cattle and European grasses caused erosion, and silt, small dams and landfill for farming raised the old salt marshes. Now the town is nearly a mile from the nearest tidal flats.

item.title: 29. Olema: coyote valley, and the ranches coming out
item.description:
This crossroads is Olema, from a Coast Miwok name meaning coyote valley. For years people believed it was the epicenter of the 1906 earthquake, because the ground moved so much here. Scientists now think the epicenter was offshore, near Daly City.
Now some very recent news. Those green hills inside Point Reyes National Seashore have been cattle ranches for well over a century, about 28,000 acres of dairy and beef, leased back to the ranchers when the park was created. But the ranches have been accused of polluting the creeks and Tomales Bay with E. coli, and a 2022 inspection found raw sewage

item.title: 30. Point Reyes: elk, elephant seals and the foggiest lighthouse
item.description:
Out on the Point Reyes peninsula is one of the wildest corners of California, and it's full of comeback stories.
Quiz: when Europeans arrived, there were maybe half a million tule elk in California. By the 1870s, people thought they were extinct. How many were found, hiding in a marsh in the Central Valley? … A single breeding pair! In 1978, ten tule elk were brought here to Tomales Point and fenced in. They thrived, then nearly half died in the drought of 2012 to 2015, and in 2020 activists illegally carried water to them. In December 2024, the Park Service finally breached the fence, and no

item.title: 31. Riding the San Andreas Fault
item.description:
Right now we're driving almost exactly along the San Andreas Fault. This straight valley is the fault zone. To the north it sinks under Tomales Bay; to the south it runs under Bolinas Lagoon. Then it heads out to sea and comes back on land near Daly City, which we'll pass this afternoon.
Some numbers. The fault runs about 750 miles through California. The Pacific Plate, on your right, slides north about an inch a year compared with the North American Plate. But it doesn't slide smoothly. It sticks, builds up strain for decades, then lets go. In 1906, the ground along the fault shifted by up t

item.title: 32. Bolinas: the town that doesn't want to be found
item.description:
Somewhere across the lagoon is Bolinas, and you won't see a sign for it, because the locals keep tearing them down. Every road sign on Highway 1 pointing the way has been removed by residents. The county even put it to a vote, and the voters said: no more signs, thank you.
It's a famously private little town of about fourteen hundred people. It also has a great property story. In 1927, an old dairy farm on the mesa was split into more than five thousand tiny lots, and a San Francisco newspaper sold many of them for 69 dollars and fifty cents each, as a subscription promotion. Buy the paper, g

item.title: 33. Stinson Beach and the craziest race in America
item.description:
Stinson Beach! A long sandy beach that San Franciscans have been escaping to for 150 years. It started as Willow Camp, tents among the willows. After the 1906 earthquake, refugees from the city came out and opened some of its first businesses, and in 1916 it was renamed after the biggest landowners, Rose and Nathan Stinson.
Sports fans: this is the finish line of the Dipsea, the oldest trail race in America. Since 1905, runners have raced seven and a half miles from Mill Valley, over the shoulder of Mount Tam, to this beach, with about 2,200 feet of climbing. You can take shortcuts with names

item.title: 34. Mount Tam: the crookedest railroad and the first mountain bikes
item.description:
The big mountain above us is Mount Tamalpais, Mount Tam to the locals, 2,571 feet at the East Peak.
Myth-busting first. You'll hear that Tamalpais means Sleeping Maiden, from a Miwok legend about the mountain's profile. It doesn't. That legend was invented in Victorian times by a playwright, for a play at the mountain's outdoor theatre. The name really comes from the Coast Miwok támal pájis, meaning west hill.
From 1896 to 1930, a railway wound up from Mill Valley to the summit, with so many bends it was nicknamed the Crookedest Railroad in the World.
And here's one for sports fans: this mo

item.title: 35. Coast redwoods: the tallest living things on Earth
item.description:
Five things about coast redwoods.
One: they're the tallest living trees on Earth. The record holder, up in Humboldt County, is about 381 feet.
Two: they can live about 2,000 years and grow 29 feet across.
Three: they only grow in a narrow strip along the coast, from south of Big Sur up to the corner of Oregon, because they need fog. In dry summers they drink moisture straight out of the air.
Four: before the Gold Rush they covered about two million acres. Today only about five percent of the old-growth forest is left.
And five: the oldest, tallest trees tend to survive in deep, steep cany

item.title: 36. Muir Woods: the man who gave away a forest
item.description:
Welcome to Muir Woods, one of the last old-growth redwood forests in the Bay Area, in a canyon on the side of Mount Tam that's wrapped in fog all summer. The redwoods drink that fog during the dry season.
Here's how it survived. Mount Tam's redwoods were logged heavily to build San Francisco, and again to rebuild it after 1906. But the trees in this canyon were too hard to reach. In 1905, William Kent and his wife Elizabeth bought 611 acres of it for 45,000 dollars, with money borrowed from a banker friend. Then a water company tried to take part of it to build a dam and reservoir. So Kent us

item.title: 37. Muir Woods and the founding of the United Nations
item.description:
One more Muir Woods story. In April 1945, delegates from 50 countries gathered in San Francisco to write the Charter of the United Nations. President Franklin Roosevelt was due to open the conference, but he died on the 12th of April, just before it began. So on the 19th of May, the delegates came out here to Cathedral Grove and held a ceremony in his memory among the redwoods, and left a plaque in his honour. It's still there.
And a practical note: Muir Woods gets up to six thousand visitors a day at peak times, and since 2018 you need a reservation to park or take the shuttle.

item.title: 38. The Olympics that came out of nowhere
item.description:
Skiers, this one's for you. If you live in San Francisco, your nearest big mountains are around Lake Tahoe. And the biggest ski resort there has quite a story.
In 1956, Squaw Valley had one chairlift, two rope tows and a fifty-room lodge. And yet it won the right to host the 1960 Winter Olympics. Its founder, Alexander Cushing, sold it as a blank canvas, and California poured in money for roads, bridges, water and power. At the 1956 Games, there wasn't even a mayor to hand the Olympic flag to, because Squaw Valley wasn't a town. The 1960 Games were the first Winter Olympics televised live, wi

item.title: 39. Mill Valley, Chief Marin and the Blind Pig
item.description:
This junction, where Highway 1 meets 101, sits at the edge of Mill Valley, the town tucked into the redwood canyons on Mount Tam.
People have lived here a very long time. Fourteen Coast Miwok village sites have been found around Mill Valley, with huge shell mounds along Richardson Bay. One, dug up in 1907, was twenty feet high. A plaque in a Mill Valley pavement marks the spot believed to be Chief Marin's birthplace, in 1781.
And right around this intersection, in 1916, a roadhouse called the Blind Pig was built just outside the town limits, where the dry laws weren't enforced as strictly. D

item.title: 40. Sausalito: streets under the bay
item.description:
Down to the left is Sausalito, on Richardson Bay. The name is Spanish for little willow grove, and it's been spelled about a dozen ways over the years.
Before the bridge, Sausalito was the end of the line. Trains from up north, including that North Pacific Coast Railroad from the Russian River, met the ferries here. The car ferry to San Francisco took about twenty minutes and cost a dollar a car. In World War Two it became a shipbuilding town, and afterwards it went arty and wealthy, and famous for its houseboats.
Quiz: when Sausalito was laid out, planners assumed it would grow by filling i

item.title: 41. The Marin Headlands: the city that never got built
item.description:
Those wild green hills on the right are the Marin Headlands. They look untouched, but they came close to becoming a city.
In the 1960s, the government sold more than 2,000 acres here to a developer who planned a new town called Marincello, for 30,000 people, in 50 apartment towers, with housing estates, a shopping centre and a hotel. In 1970 the developer lost a lawsuit, and the land went to the Golden Gate National Recreation Area instead.
The hills are also full of old forts and gun batteries from the 1890s to World War Two, built to keep enemy ships out of the bay, plus a Cold War Nike mi

item.title: 42. The Golden Gate Bridge
item.description:
Here it is, everyone! The Golden Gate Bridge! Cameras out, passengers.
When it opened in 1937, it was the longest and tallest suspension bridge in the world: towers 746 feet tall, a main span of 4,200 feet. Plenty of experts said it couldn't be built at all, because of the wind, the fog and the tides.
Quiz: the colour is International Orange, chosen by the architect Irving Morrow. But the US Navy wanted something more visible to ships. What did they suggest? … Black and yellow stripes! A giant bumblebee. Thank goodness for Morrow.
Some infrastructure numbers for the engineers in the car. Th

item.title: 43. How the bridge was paid for, and why Marin has no BART
item.description:
Now the economics. After the 1929 crash, the bridge district couldn't sell its 30-million-dollar bond issue. Then in 1932, Amadeo Giannini, founder of Bank of America, agreed to buy the whole lot to help the local economy. And the bonds were paid off in 1971, entirely from tolls.
Those tolls, charged on the southbound side only, are still the district's main income, and that had a big side effect. In the 1950s and 60s, the district opposed running BART trains across the bridge, because it didn't want to lose toll money. That helped push Marin County out of the BART system altogether. So the r

item.title: 44. The Presidio, and the greatest comeback in sailing
item.description:
Off the end of the bridge we're driving through the Presidio, a military base for 219 years. The Spanish founded it in 1776, the same year as the American Declaration of Independence, then it passed to Mexico, then to the US Army in 1848, and in 1994 to the National Park Service. Lucasfilm now has its headquarters here. And the road you're on, the Presidio Parkway, replaced an old viaduct that wasn't safe in an earthquake. It cost 1.1 billion dollars, and the tunnels have a 14-acre park on their roof called Presidio Tunnel Tops.
Down on the water is where the 2013 America's Cup was raced, in

item.title: 45. Golden Gate Park and the world’s weirdest race
item.description:
Nineteenth Avenue runs right through Golden Gate Park: 1,017 acres and about 24 million visitors a year. It was built from the 1870s on the Outside Lands, and three-quarters of it was sand dunes. Engineer William Hammond Hall and gardener John McLaren spent years planting grass and trees to hold the sand in place. At the ocean end there are two Dutch-style windmills from 1903 that used to pump water around the park.
And this is where one of the world's weirdest races finishes. Bay to Breakers started on New Year's Day 1912, to show the rest of the country, buried in snow, that San Francisco w

item.title: 46. San Francisco: Gold Rush ships to the richest city in America
item.description:
Welcome to San Francisco, Julia's home turf. A bit of its story, by the numbers.
1847: the town was a little trading post called Yerba Buena, with about 459 people. That January, its American mayor renamed it San Francisco, partly because General Vallejo was planning a town called Francisca after his wife. San Francisco grabbed the name, so Vallejo's town became Benicia.
1848 to 1849: the Gold Rush. From about 1,000 people to 25,000 in under two years. Ships' crews deserted to go dig for gold, leaving around 500 empty ships in the harbour. Some became warehouses, saloons and hotels, and some

item.title: 47. Mike’s corner: the delivery wars
item.description:
Mike, this one's for you. You're driving through the home turf of your biggest rivals.
In January 2013, four Stanford students launched a site called PaloAltoDelivery.com, down the Peninsula in Palo Alto. That summer, the startup accelerator Y Combinator gave them 120,000 dollars for seven percent of the company, and they renamed it DoorDash. Today DoorDash has 56 percent of the American food delivery market, it entered the Fortune 500 in 2024, and through Deliveroo and Wolt it now operates all over Europe, including, of course, the UK.
Meanwhile, from your side of the Atlantic: in 2020, Jus

item.title: 48. 5:12 a.m., April 18, 1906
item.description:
Story time: the morning San Francisco fell down. At 5:12 a.m. on the 18th of April, 1906, the San Andreas Fault ruptured along about 280 miles of coast, the same fault we followed past Tomales Bay and Bolinas this morning. A foreshock first, then about 42 seconds of violent shaking. Magnitude about 7.9.
Then came the fires, burning for days. More than 3,000 people died, the deadliest earthquake in American history, and over 80 percent of the city was destroyed. At the time, San Francisco was the biggest city on the West Coast.

item.title: 49. Daly City: little boxes on the hillside
item.description:
We're crossing into Daly City. After the 1906 earthquake, thousands of homeless San Franciscans headed south to the ranches here, including one belonging to John Daly, a dairyman who had married his boss's daughter. The town grew out of those refugees and took his name.
From the late 1940s, developer Henry Doelger built Westlake, one of the first big planned suburbs, with rows and rows of near-identical houses up the hills. It inspired Malvina Reynolds' 1962 folk song Little Boxes, which pokes fun at exactly that.

item.title: 50. Colma: where the dead outnumber the living
item.description:
Here's the strangest town of the whole trip: Colma. Most of its land is cemeteries.
In 1900, San Francisco banned new burials in the city, and in 1912 it evicted most of its existing cemeteries. About 150,000 bodies were dug up and moved down here, at ten dollars per grave. Nearly everyone famous who died in San Francisco ended up here.
Quiz: the dead here outnumber the living. By roughly how much? … About a thousand to one! There are around one and a half million people buried in Colma. It's been called the City of the Silent, and its unofficial motto is: It's great to be alive in Colma.

item.title: 51. Discovering San Francisco Bay
item.description:
On the hills to the west is Sweeney Ridge, where Europeans first laid eyes on San Francisco Bay.
In 1769, a Spanish expedition under Gaspar de Portolá was heading up the coast. Portolá sent scouts under Sergeant José Ortega north to find the Point Reyes headlands, which we drove past this morning. Ortega came back and said he couldn't get there, because the Golden Gate was in the way. And from Sweeney Ridge, on the 4th of November 1769, the expedition saw San Francisco Bay, although the scouts had spotted it a few days before.

item.title: 52. San Andreas Lake: Yosemite in your tap
item.description:
Off to the right, just south of here, is San Andreas Lake, the lake in the valley that gave the San Andreas Fault its name. The fault runs straight down it, and its earth dam, built in 1868, sits right on top of the fault. It survived 1906.
It's also part of one of the great feats of American water engineering. Julia, your tap water in San Francisco comes from Yosemite. The Hetch Hetchy Valley was dammed under a law passed in 1913, the Raker Act, after a huge political fight. item.title: 53. SFO: from cow pasture to the world
item.description:
And here we are: San Francisco International. Last quiz of the trip: when the city opened its airport here in May 1927, what was the land being used for? … It was a cow pasture! 150 acres, leased from the Mills family as a temporary, experimental airfield called Mills Field. The city bought it in 1931, and the word International was added after World War Two. Funny detail: it's owned by San Francisco, but it's actually in San Mateo County.
